extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of communication, journalism, and political/media researchers studying news coverage and content analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis rubric and methodological standards for measuring who voices opinion, the direction of those opinions, and the degree to which press/editorial opinion is 'indexed' to official institutional conflict; applied to New York Times coverage of Nicaragua (1983–1986).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing hypothesis (criterion for explaining coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists implicitly answer what, how much, and whose opinion to cover by looking to 'official' conflict or opposition levels within the government — i.e., news and editorial opinion will be 'indexed' to levels of official (primarily congressional) opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing compresses public opinion to fit the range of debate between decisive institutional power blocs; observed as tight correspondence between congressional opposition reported in news and op-ed editorial opposition (e.g., correlations r = .63 to .76). Use changes in official opposition as a primary explanatory variable for news and editorial opinion shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection: news organ exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the New York Times as the sample source: all news articles and editorials indexed under 'Nicaragua' in the New York Times Index between January 1, 1983 and October 15, 1986 (supplement with Lexis/Nexis where Index omissions occur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the Times cues other outlets and is a 'self-conscious keeper' of the national record; when full mass-media coverage is impractical, analyze a leading paper as a critical test case (especially if it has a known editorial stance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of coding: opinion-voiced determination from index abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the abstract of every story/editorial in the NYT Index and judge whether an opinion was voiced on the policy issue; if so, code who voiced it and the direction of the opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index abstracts are suitable because the Index was constructed primarily around 'who said what' and often contains extensive summaries; this makes coding straightforward and reliable for large populations of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice categories (who voiced the opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign opinions to categories of 'voice': editorial and op-ed, administration source, congressional source, judicial source, popular (nongovernmental, including interest groups and polls), and foreign opinion from U.S. allies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sandinista and contra opinions were assigned 'no valence' (canceled out) when analyzing a domestic U.S. policy process; ensure category definitions match the political frame of the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence coding (direction of opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valence assigned as '+' if the voice supported administration contra policy, '-' if the voice opposed contra policy, and '±' if the voice was ambivalent or divided about the policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply valence to the voice as reported (e.g., congressional vote summarized as a 'victory' → Congress coded '+'); resolve ambiguous/split reports as '±' or coded by mutual agreement among coders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal weighting of voices (coding weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the primary analysis, all coded voices are weighted the same: e.g., the President is given the same weight as an undersecretary, a poll, or a grass-roots statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speech by a senator is coded as a single 'voice'; a Senate roll-call vote is coded as a single voice when summarized in terms of policy outcome; articles that present multiple policy positions should be coded as multiple voices. Simplicity in weighting aids reliability and serves as a first test; more sophisticated weighting can be considered later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-coding articles with multiple voices
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article documents competing positions (e.g., a battle between the President and House Speaker), code the article for each distinct voice it reports (e.g., 'administration' and 'congressional' both get coded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles describing different policy positions are double-coded (or multi-coded) to reflect the plurality of voices represented; this preserves the 'who said what' nature of coverage in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of foreign and partisan belligerent voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign Sandinista and contra opinions 'no valence' (i.e., cancel them out) when the focus is on domestic U.S. policy debate and relative domestic supportability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the external actors' opinions are approximately balanced, canceling them out is acceptable; explicitly document this decision because it affects interpretation of domestic voice distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval and inclusion of polls (when index omits them)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the primary index undercounts a category (e.g., opinion polls), retrieve them systematically from full-text databases (e.g., Lexis/Nexis) and include them in the 'popular' voice category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the extent of index omission (the NYT Index omitted a substantial percentage of opinion polls) and correct for it by supplementary searches to avoid systematic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of congressional (official) opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate official opposition (primarily congressional) as the number of voices, votes, and journalistic characterizations of opposition from members and voting blocs in Congress as a percent of the total of all opinions expressed in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label figures as 'congressional opposition' when the majority of official opposition originates in Congress; use this measure as the baseline for indexing comparisons with editorial opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of editorial opposition (two variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Net editorial opposition: (con editorials and op-ed pieces) minus (pro editorials and op-ed pieces). 2) Total opposition voices on op-ed/editorial pages as a percentage of all opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use net opposition for conceptual/theoretical analyses (readers/editors approach editorial content differently and net departures signal change). Use total-opposition-voices % as a robustness check (produced a stronger indexing coefficient in this study). Net measure is more stable with small editorial counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal partitioning: episode intervals tied to policy actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the study period into intervals corresponding to episodes climaxed by key policy votes in Congress (17 intervals used for the three-year period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing time around culminating congressional actions allows observation of opinion variation during periods of congressional activity versus inactivity; small number of intervals (n=17) cautions against overreliance on inferential statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic caution on statistical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the small number of total intervals, avoid overreliance on conventional statistical testing; emphasize structural and graphically visible patterns and build confidence via multiple consistent indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Pearson correlation coefficients for key associations (they can be informative) but interpret them alongside visual and structural evidence rather than as sole proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of coding to maximize intercoder reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the coding scheme as simple as possible (e.g., simple voice/valence codes) to achieve high intercoder reliability; in this study two coders achieved 98% agreement on the initial opinion/no-opinion task and .94 on opinion voice and valence codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve discrepancies by mutual agreement; document clerical errors separately; simple coding schemes permit reliable first tests and indicate whether more sophisticated coding is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Index as an appropriate coding source
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on the newspaper's index abstracts for coding when the Index contains detailed 'who said what' summaries, making it 'ideal' for coding opinions voiced in news and editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate index suitability by spot-checking full text (e.g., via Lexis/Nexis) and retrieve categories undercounted by the Index (polls) as needed; document validation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive standard: editorial pages vs news pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat editorial/op-ed content as conceptually different from news content: editorial pages contain obligatory or expected balance and departures from a paper's typical pro/con balance are the best indicators of a news organization's change in editorial thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer net editorial-opposition measures for tracking editorial shifts; compare editorial measures to news-reported official opposition to test indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative diagnostic: marginalization of popular opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the press marginalizes nongovernmental 'popular' voices (e.g., polls, grassroots protest) relative to official institutional voices; evidence of marginalization supports the indexing critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document frequency and prominence (e.g., headline vs back-page mentions) of polls and popular voices and assess whether press attention changes over time independent of public opinion trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue-area expectation for indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect indexing to operate most consistently in issue areas tied to state and corporate power (military decisions, foreign affairs, trade, macroeconomic policy), where authoritative institutional divisions are pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying other issue domains, assess whether clear institutional power blocs exist; absent such clear divisions, indexing may be weaker or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms and paths for change in indexing norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider external triggers (market decline for hard news, loss of public confidence, societal political shifts) and three institutional change paths: corporate/boardroom reforms, professional/normative debate in newsrooms and journalism schools, and initiatives by individual reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which path(s) are plausible in the case being studied; document structural barriers that make change unlikely under current profitability and normative conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of coding disagreements and reliability statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report intercoder reliability metrics and describe the kinds of disagreements (clerical error vs substantive valence interpretation) and how they were resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliability figures to justify coding simplicity and to argue whether more sophisticated schemes are warranted; explicitly report procedures for resolving valence disagreements.
